title: From 54 New Cases in July to Zero in August: TCI’s COVID Turnaround
content: Turks and Caicos Islands reported zero new COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, or deaths between August 17 and 23, 2025, marking a dramatic turnaround from mid-July 2025, when 54 new cases were recorded in a single week. The total confirmed cases since 2020 stand at 6,922, with 6,866 recoveries and 41 deaths. Health officials attribute the decline to sustained public vigilance, accessible free testing, and widespread vaccination at government clinics. Despite the encouraging data, the Ministry of Health urges continued caution, recommending handwashing, mask-wearing in crowded spaces, protecting vulnerable populations, and maintaining up-to-date vaccinations. The shift from a peak of 54 cases in July to zero in August reflects a significant improvement, signaling that the pandemic is no longer a disruptive force in the islands. The Ministry released the bulletin on September 2, 2025, emphasizing that while the situation remains stable, the fight is not over.

title: Luxusinsel Turks- und Caicos kämpft mit extremer Gewaltkriminalität
content:
The Turks and Caicos Islands, once famed for their pristine beaches and affluent tourism, are now grappling with an unprecedented surge in violent crime. In the past year, 48 murders were recorded—an alarming figure that translates to the highest murder rate in the Caribbean and Latin America for a population of fewer than 50,000 people. By mid‑August 2025, 24 of those deaths had already occurred, and the first mass shooting in the islands’ history took place in July, claiming four lives and injuring nine others. 

BBC reports highlight the growing fear among residents. Pastor Jacques Phanor told the BBC, 'Die Menschen haben große Angst. Einige ziehen sogar weg. Wir lieben die Inseln, die Wirtschaft ist gut, aber das Kriminalitätsumfeld ist furchtbar.' He also points to Haitian migrants fleeing violence in their homeland as a contributing factor, adding, 'Die Kriminalität ist in den haitianischen Gemeinden schlimmer.' The government has responded with temporary curfews, stricter bar and restaurant controls, and enhanced police powers; informal settlements identified as criminal hubs were partially cleared in August. Premier Washington Misick appealed to the Haitian community, saying, 'diese Inseln sicher zu halten,' while the UK government invested nine million pounds in coastal surveillance and investigative resources.

Despite the escalating violence, tourism remains the islands’ economic backbone, generating approximately 250 million dollars in the first half of the 2024/25 fiscal year. Wilkie Arthur, a former inmate who served eleven years for armed robbery, now works as a reporter and cautions, 'Viele Menschen wollen nicht in Gangs sein, sie finden einfach keine Arbeit. Wir müssen sie stärken, damit sie nicht jemanden wegen ein paar Dollar ausrauben müssen.'

A 2024 UN report notes a broader regional trend of rising organized crime and lethal violence, driven by increased drug production in South America and widespread firearm availability. In contrast, Aruba enjoys a low crime rate and strict security protocols, ranking far ahead in the Caribbean Island Safety Index 2025.

title: Los ahogamientos se cobran la vida de 48 personas en Canarias hasta...
content: Between January and September 2025, 48 people died from drowning in the Canary Islands, a decrease of three deaths (-6%) compared to the same period in 2024, according to data compiled by the association 'Canarias, 1500 km de Costa' for aquatic accident prevention. The most recent incident occurred on Monday, September 29, when two men went missing in southern Gran Canaria: Layonel Ramírez, a 30-year-old man, disappeared after diving into the sea to retrieve his drifting personal watercraft near Castillo del Romeral in San Bartolomé de Tirajana, during nighttime conditions. The second case involved a swimmer who vanished off the coast of Mogán late at night, though one of the two companions managed to escape the water. In September alone, 26 people were affected by aquatic accidents, including nine fatalities—matching the number of deaths in August and surpassing January (8), April (5), and May (5). September also recorded two critically injured, two severely injured, six moderately injured, three lightly injured, and two rescued without injury. The monthly average of drowning deaths in the Canary Islands has stabilized at five per month, down from six in 2024. From January to September, in addition to the 48 fatalities, 11 swimmers were treated in critical condition, 19 with severe injuries, 45 with moderate injuries, 15 with minor injuries, and 15 rescued unharmed—totaling 154 people involved in aquatic incidents. Among these, 15 minors were affected, four of whom died; one was in critical condition, four had severe injuries, five had moderate injuries, and one was rescued without harm. Of the 48 fatalities, 36% (17) were adult swimmers, 31% (15) were over 60 years old, and 25% (12) had unknown ages. Nationality data show 10 of the deceased were foreign nationals: 4 British, 2 Polish, 1 Italian, 3 without specified nationality, 2 Spanish, and 3 with unknown nationality. The majority of victims were male (73%, or 35), with 27% (13) being female. The association identifies 'imprudence' as the primary cause: 40% of fatal victims and 35% of all affected individuals entered the water during pre-alerts or active alerts issued by the Government of Canarias due to adverse coastal conditions. Additionally, 8% of fatalities occurred during heatwave warnings. The majority of deaths (67%, or 32) were swimmers, followed by 17% (8) being fishermen, 14% (7) with no recorded activity at the time of death, and 2% (1) classified as 'others'—including accidental falls from piers, cliffs, seafront promenades, or from paragliders, pilots, boat crew, and others. By island, Tenerife recorded the highest number of drownings (14), followed by Gran Canaria (13), Lanzarote (7), Fuerteventura (6), La Gomera and El Hierro (3 each), and La Palma (2). Beaches were the most common site of incidents (54%), followed by ports/coastal zones (19%), natural pools (17%), and swimming pools (10%). Most incidents (67%) occurred in the afternoon, 23% in the morning, and 2% at night, with 8% having unspecified timing. The association is supported by the Gran Canaria Cabildo, the Elder Museum of Science and Technology, the Government of Canarias' Department of Territorial Policy, Cohesion, and Water, the Las Palmas de Gran Canaria City Council’s Tourism and Maritime City departments, and Binter.

title: Paradise Fights to Stay Safe as Turks and Caicos Battles Rising Crime
content: The Turks and Caicos Islands, long celebrated for turquoise waters and postcard sunsets, are now grappling with a surge in violent crime, migration pressures, and political strain.  The territory recorded 48 homicides last year—its highest per‑capita murder rate—and by mid‑August 2024 an additional 24 killings had already occurred, including the first mass shooting in island history when gunmen stormed a bar, killing four and wounding nine.  Pastor Jacques Phanor, a long‑time Providenciales resident, told BBC reporters, 'People are terrified. Some are even leaving. We all love the islands, the economy is good, but the crime environment is terrible.'  Premier Washington Misick blamed the July massacre on Haitian gang influence, calling it a 'gangland‑type slaying' and urging Haitian leaders to help 'keep these islands safe.'  The Haitian Heritage Association condemned these 'hateful narratives,' stressing that most Haitians on the islands are law‑abiding.  Phanor, who was born in Haiti but is a citizen of Turks and Caicos, noted that many of this year’s victims were Haitian and that children born to undocumented parents often fall through legal cracks, becoming easy targets for gangs.  Despite the violence, tourism remains strong: nearly two million visitors arrived in 2024, generating more than $250 million in just six months.  Local journalist Wilkie Arthur, formerly jailed for armed robbery, said, 'Many people don’t even want to be in gangs; they just can’t find work. We need to empower them so they won’t have to rob someone for a couple of dollars.'  Authorities have imposed curfews, restricted alcohol sales, and demolished over 220 shanties in August alone, while the UK has pledged £9 million for coastal surveillance and patrol boats.  Tourism Minister Zhavargo Jolly acknowledged crime as a 'concern' but insisted the islands would remain 'not only one of the world’s most beautiful destinations, but also a safe and welcoming place for all to visit.'  The article presents a balanced account of rising crime, political responses, and the resilience of local communities, citing statistics, direct quotes, and policy measures.

title: Mueren ahogadas 48 personas en Canarias en lo que va de año
content: The organization 'Canarias, 1.500 km de costa' reported that 48 people have died from drowning in the Canary Islands during the first nine months of 2025, three fewer than the same period in 2024. The primary cause of these aquatic accidents is imprudence, with 40% of fatal victims and 35% of all affected individuals entering the sea during pre-alerts or active alerts issued by the Canarian government due to adverse coastal conditions. On September 30, two young people went missing in separate incidents in southern Gran Canaria: Layonel Ramírez, a 30-year-old local, disappeared while trying to retrieve his drifting personal watercraft; the second case involved a swimmer who vanished during the early hours of Monday in Mogán, with only one of two companions surviving. In September alone, there were 26 incidents resulting in 9 deaths (matching the peak of August), 2 critical cases, 2 severe injuries, 6 moderate injuries, 3 minor injuries, and 2 rescues. The monthly average of drowning deaths has decreased to 5 per month (down from 6 in 2024). Overall, 154 people were involved in aquatic accidents in 2025, including 15 minors (4 fatalities, 1 critical, 4 severe, 5 moderate, 1 rescued unharmed). Of the 48 fatalities, 35 were male (73%), 13 were female (27%), 17 were adult swimmers (36%), 15 were over 60 (31%), and 12 had unknown age (25%). Among the deceased, 10 were foreign nationals: 4 British, 2 Polish, 1 Italian, 3 without specified nationality, 2 Spanish, and 3 with unknown nationality. Tenerife recorded the highest number of drownings (14), followed by Gran Canaria (13), Lanzarote (7), Fuerteventura (6), La Gomera and El Hierro (3 each), and La Palma (2). The most common accident locations were beaches (54%), coastal ports/zones (19%), natural pools (17%), and artificial pools (10). Most incidents occurred in the afternoon (67%), followed by morning (23%), night (2%), and 8% with unspecified timing.

title: Canarias suma este verano 51 muertes por culpa del calor, el doble que en 2024
content: According to the MoMo system, managed by the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII), there have been 51 deaths in the Canary Islands due to high temperatures this summer, doubling the number of deaths from the same period last year (26 estimated). The majority of deaths occurred in the episodes of high temperatures that began on July 17 and ended on July 26 (36 deaths), and from August 10 to 18 (15 deaths). The heatwave in August, which saw temperatures above 40 degrees for several days, particularly in Gran Canaria, and a calima episode, has left 15 victims. Of the 15 deaths in August, 14 were over 65 years old, with 3 between 74 and 85 years old and 7 over 85 years old. The MoMo system estimates that in the entire summer, 2,635 people have died due to high temperatures in Spain, a 40% increase from the same period last year. The majority of deaths were people over 65 years old (2,529), with 2,347 being 75 or older. The heatwave in August has left more than 100 victims per day, with the highest number of deaths on August 17 (125). The temperatures have killed people indirectly by aggravating pre-existing conditions in the elderly and vulnerable, and directly through heatstroke, with at least 23 deaths in the summer, compared to 17 in 2024.

title: Canarias suma 51 muertes por culpa del calor en lo que va de verano
content: According to the MoMo system, which monitors daily mortality, 51 deaths in the Canary Islands and 2,635 deaths in Spain can be attributed to high temperatures this summer. The majority of the victims were over 65 years old, with 2,347 deaths occurring among those aged 75 and over. The system estimates that 1,579 women and 1,056 men died due to heat, with a 40% increase in heat-related deaths compared to the same period last year. The heat wave that started on August 3 and ended on August 19 was particularly deadly, with 1,149 heat-related deaths recorded during this period. At least 23 people have died from heat stroke, four of whom were working at the time of their death. This number has already surpassed the number of heat stroke deaths recorded in the entire summer of 2024 and 2022, and is approaching the record set in 2023, when 24 people died from heat stroke.

title: Canarias cierra el verano con 12 personas fallecidas por...
content: Canarias closed the summer with 12 drownings, a 20% drop from the previous year (15). In 2023, 11 deaths were recorded, while 2022 and 2020 each had 12, and 2021 had nine. The monthly average for the first eight months of 2025 was five deaths; July saw three, and August the highest monthly figure with nine. By island, Tenerife, Fuerteventura and Lanzarote each reported three deaths, Gran Canaria two, and El Hierro one. A total of 50 people suffered accidents in beaches, pools and natural pools during the summer, including four rescued from the sea in critical condition, 11 seriously injured, 20 with moderate injuries and three with mild injuries, setting a new record for affected individuals in the last five years. Only in the two summer months were eight minors victims of aquatic accidents, with one fatality, three serious injuries and four moderate injuries. Tenerife and Fuerteventura each had three minors, Gran Canaria two. Minor accidents occurred in four pools, two beaches and two natural pools. The platform notes that 90% of child drownings result from negligence, 'producto de una falta de atención y vigilancia de los adultos a su cargo', and cites the initiative as supported by the Cabildo de Gran Canaria, Museo Elder de la Ciencia y la Tecnología, Viceconsejería de Actividad Física y Deportes, and other regional bodies.
